In Praise of Wandering: Attention, Time, and the Quiet Art of Being Alive

I want to begin with something small. Not a grand thesis or a breaking discovery, but a chipped blue mug on my desk, half full of cold tea. The morning light comes through the window at a slant this time of year, and it catches the steam — except there is no steam anymore, because I forgot to drink it while it was hot. I forgot because I was watching dust.

That sounds ridiculous, but it's true. A single shaft of sunlight had turned the ordinary air in my room into a slow snow globe. Dust motes turning, drifting, glowing. I have lived in rooms with sunlight for more than three decades, and I have seen dust a thousand times, and yet this morning it stopped me. It was beautiful in a way that felt almost private, like the world had leaned in to whisper something it only says when you're not in a hurry.

We don't get many of those moments anymore, not because the world stopped offering them, but because we stopped being available to receive them. So if I get to write freely, for a long while, this is what I want to write about: the strange, ordinary miracle of paying attention. Of wandering. Of being a human creature hurtling through time on a spinning rock and occasionally, miraculously, noticing.

There is a particular kind of wandering that has nothing to do with travel. You can do it sitting still. You can do it washing dishes or waiting for a train or lying awake at 3 a.m. while the house creaks. It's mental wandering, yes, but it's also something more generous than that word implies. Daydreaming sounds frivolous. Mind-wandering sounds like a failure of focus. But what I'm talking about is actually a form of attention — a wide, soft, open attention that doesn't clutch at anything, but lets things come.

We are taught from childhood to pay the narrow kind of attention. Focus. Concentrate. Zero in. Keep your eyes on the prize, on the test, on the road. And that kind of attention is useful. It's how you do surgery and land planes and finish exams. But it's not the only kind, and I worry we've started to treat it as if it were.

There is also the attention of the poet and the child and the naturalist and the lover: the attention that widens instead of narrows. The attention that notices the way the cashier's voice lifts when she laughs, the way pigeons tilt their heads in perfect synchrony, the way rain smells different on hot concrete than it does on grass. This attention doesn't produce anything. It doesn't optimize or monetize. It just witnesses. And in witnessing, it honors.

I think we are starving for that kind of attention, both giving it and receiving it. To be truly noticed — not photographed, not scanned, not evaluated, but noticed — is one of the rarest gifts one human can give another. When was the last time someone looked at you without glancing at a screen in between? When was the last time you looked at a tree long enough to see it as an individual, not just “a tree,” but this particular tree, with its lean to the left and its scar where a branch was lost and its stubborn cluster of last year's leaves still clinging on in spring?

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. I keep returning to that line. It reframes everything. Attention isn't just a cognitive resource to be managed for productivity. It's a moral act. It's how we say: you matter enough for me to set aside my noise for a moment and let you be real to me.

And what is true for people is true for moments, too. Mornings matter. Tea matters. Dust matters, if you let it.

Let me wander a little further, into time.

Time is the strangest thing we live inside and never understand. Physicists will tell you it's a dimension, philosophers will tell you it's an illusion, and your grandmother will tell you it flies when you're having fun and crawls when you're in the dentist's chair. All of them are right.

I have a theory that we don't live in time the way we think we do. We live in stories about time. Childhood feels long in retrospect because everything was new; novelty stretches memory. A summer when you're nine contains first swims and bee stings and a friend's backyard and a thunderstorm that knocked out the power — a hundred firsts packed into ten weeks. A summer when you're thirty-nine can pass in a blink because you did the same commute and ate the same lunch and scrolled the same feed. The clock measured the same hours, but your memory measured something entirely different.

This is why wandering matters. Newness slows time. Attention stretches it. When you take a different route home, when you actually taste your food, when you listen to a stranger's story on a bus, you are laying down denser memory. You are making your life longer from the inside.

I once read about a man who decided to conduct an experiment: for a month, he would do one small new thing every day. Not skydive or quit his job, just small: take a different street, try a fruit he'd never tried, listen to a genre he thought he hated, talk to a neighbor he'd only nodded at. At the end of the month he swore the month had felt like three months long. His life hadn't changed in any external way, but internally it had thickened. It had texture again.

I think of that often when days start to blur. The antidote to the blur isn't necessarily a vacation or a major life overhaul, though those have their place. Sometimes it's just deliberate noticing. Cook something with a spice you can't pronounce. Learn the name of the bird that sings outside your window at dawn — it's probably a robin or a wren or a mockingbird, depending where you live, and once you know its name you'll hear it differently. Sit on a bench for ten minutes with no phone and just watch how people walk. Everyone has a walk, a signature rhythm. Hurried, shuffling, bouncy, weary. You can read whole biographies in gait if you're patient.

Memory, of course, is wandering's twin sister.

We tend to think of memory as a filing cabinet, a place where the past is stored. But neuroscientists now tell us it's more like a story we retell every time, editing slightly with each telling. Every time you remember your tenth birthday party, you're not pulling up a video file; you're reconstructing it from fragments, filling gaps with plausible details, tinting it with how you feel today. Memory is creative. Memory is alive.

That's a little terrifying and also deeply hopeful. It means the past isn't fixed. Not the facts — those happened — but the meaning. A painful memory revisited with kinder eyes, ten years later, can soften. A happy memory savored can deepen. We are not just archivists of our lives; we are authors, constantly revising.

I love eavesdropping on my own old memories. The smell of my elementary school hallway — pencil shavings and floor wax and milk cartons. The particular squeak of my father's shoes on the kitchen linoleum on Saturday mornings when he made pancakes. The way my best friend in high school used to tap her pen three times before answering a question she knew she would get right. None of these details mattered at the time. They were background. But now they are treasures. They are proof that I was there, that I lived, that the world was textured and specific and utterly unrepeatable.

And here's the thing: right now, you are laying down the background details that your future self will treasure. The hum of your refrigerator. The way light falls in your current kitchen. The laugh of someone you love that you hear so often you barely register it. One day, if life takes its usual course of change and loss and moving on, those sounds will be gone, and you will ache to hear them once more. So hear them now. Record them not with your phone but with your full, ridiculous, generous attention.

That brings me to strangers, because strangers are one of my favorite subjects to wander about.

Every person you pass on the street is living a life as vivid and complex as your own, with private jokes and ancient griefs and a favorite song they sing too loud in the car. There's a word for the sudden realization of this: sonder. It was coined by John Koenig in The Dictionary of Obscure Sorrows, and it names that dizzying moment when you understand that each passerby has a story you will never know.

I felt sonder intensely once on a night train. It was late, the lights were low, and across the aisle a woman was quietly crying while looking out the window. She wasn't sobbing, just leaking tears, wiping them with her sleeve, staring at black fields rushing past. I will never know what had happened — a breakup, a death, a diagnosis, a loneliness too large to name. I didn't ask; it didn't feel right to intrude. But I sat with her grief for a while in my own heart, sent her a silent wish, and then she got off at a small station and was gone. A whole novel, glimpsed for three stations.

We move through each other's lives like that all the time, mostly unaware. The barista who remembers your order is studying nursing at night and worried about her mother. The man who cut you off in traffic just got terrible news and wasn't seeing the road. The teenager with headphones blaring is listening to the same song on repeat because it's the only thing that quiets his anxiety. If we could see, even for a second, the interior weather of everyone around us, we would be so much kinder. We would forgive so much faster.

Wandering teaches you this. When you're not rushing, you start to see people as people again, not obstacles or background extras. You make eye contact. You smile. You let someone merge. Small mercies, but they ripple. Kindness is contagious in the most literal, studied way — researchers have shown that witnessing kindness makes people more likely to be kind themselves. One generous act can cascade through a community in ways you'll never trace.

I wonder sometimes what the world would look like if we measured wealth not in money or followers but in moments of sonder. How rich would the good noticers be?

Of course, I have to wander into the subject of our strange modern tools, because they are both miracle and thief.

I love the internet, truly. I love that I can video-call a friend across an ocean, that I can look up how to fix a leaky faucet at midnight, that a kid in a remote village can watch lectures from the world's best universities, that lost songs and out-of-print books can find their people again. It is a Library of Alexandria that fits in a pocket, plus a post office, plus a map of the stars.

And yet. And yet.

We built a machine for connection and then let it be tuned for compulsion. The infinite scroll was not designed for your wonder; it was designed for your staying. The notification was not designed for your joy; it was designed for your return. We carry in our pockets a slot machine that occasionally pays out in love and laughter and news, which is why it's so hard to put down.

I don't think the answer is to smash our phones or move to a cabin — though a weekend in a cabin sounds lovely. I think the answer is to become more intentional wanderers, even inside the digital world. To curate our feeds the way we'd curate a garden. To follow people who make us curious and kind, not furious and small. To leave space for boredom, because boredom is the doorway to wandering. Every great idea I have ever had came not while scrolling but while waiting, while walking, while staring out a window. The mind needs fallow time. A field planted nonstop exhausts its soil. So does a mind.

Try this, as an experiment: next time you're in line, don't pull out your phone. Just stand there. Feel your feet on the floor. Notice the magazines, the tired mother, the flickering fluorescent light, your own breathing. It will feel uncomfortable for about ninety seconds. Like an itch. Then something shifts. Your thoughts start to unspool. You remember something you meant to do. You have a funny idea. You notice you're hungry or tired or actually quite content. You return to yourself. That's wandering reclaiming its territory.

Nature, of course, is wandering's oldest home.

There is a reason hospitals put windows facing trees, that prison inmates with a view of nature get sick less often, that children play more creatively on uneven ground with sticks and stones than on flat plastic playgrounds. We are animals. We evolved under sky, among leaves, near water. Our nervous systems recognize birdsong as safety, running water as life, rustling leaves as wind, not threat. Even a few minutes outside resets something primal in us.

You don't need wilderness with a capital W. A weed pushing through a sidewalk crack is nature being defiant and hopeful. Pigeons are nature. The moon is nature, hanging there every night, mostly ignored. When did you last really look at the moon? Not glance, but look — notice its craters, its lopsided glow, the way it makes the world silver and soft? It's been there your whole life, doing its quiet work of tides and cycles, and it asks for nothing but an occasional glance upward.

I have a friend who keeps a “phenology wheel” — a circular journal where she notes what’s happening in nature each week: first buds, first robin, first frost, last leaf. It’s such a simple practice, but it tunes her to a slower clock than the news cycle. She knows when the maples will turn not because an app tells her, but because she watched them last year and the year before. She belongs to her place in a way few of us do anymore.

To belong to a place — really belong — requires wandering in it. Not driving through, but walking. Getting lost on purpose. Learning which corner smells like jasmine in June, where the best puddles form after rain, which bench gets afternoon sun in winter. Biologists call this a “home range.” Humans used to know theirs intimately: where to find water, which plants healed, where the deer crossed. Now our home range is often a triangle of home, work, store, and everything else is blur. Reclaiming it, foot by foot, is a quiet revolution.

Creativity, too, lives on wandering.

We mythologize creativity as lightning bolts and tortured genius, but most creativity is just attention plus connection. You notice two things that seemed unrelated and you put them together. Penicillin was mold plus curiosity. The novel was gossip plus imagination. Every collage, recipe, business, song is recombination. And recombination requires a rich store of noticed things to recombine.

That's why artists keep sketchbooks and writers keep notebooks and scientists keep field journals. Not because every scribble is gold, but because the habit of noticing builds a compost heap. Ideas rot down, mix, warm up, and suddenly something sprouts. But if you never collect the leaves, you have no compost.

So collect. Write down overheard sentences. Sketch bad drawings of your coffee cup. Record voice memos of half-thoughts while walking. Photograph strange shadows. Keep lists: ten things that are blue today, five sounds you can hear right now, three things you believed as a child. None of this has to be good. It just has to be yours. Wandering on paper.

And then share, sometimes. Creativity completes itself in community. A story unread is a letter unsent. It doesn't need a million readers; it needs one true reader who says, “Me too. I thought I was the only one.” That’s how loneliness shrinks.

Which brings me, finally, to kindness, because what else is all this noticing for if not to love better?

There is a quiet, almost invisible kindness that never makes headlines: the friend who remembers the date of your mother’s death and texts that morning. The neighbor who shovels your walk without being asked. The teacher who stays five minutes late to explain again. The stranger who returns your lost wallet with everything intact and a little note: “Glad you got it back.” These acts don’t change the world in the sweeping sense. They change it in the only sense that lasts — person to person, heart to heart.

I think the future, if we have a good one, will not be built only by grand policies and technologies, though we need those. It will be built by millions of small attentions: people who noticed a problem on their block and cared enough to act, people who listened across difference instead of shouting, people who chose repair over discard — of objects, of relationships, of ecosystems.

Hope gets a bad rap as naive. But real hope isn’t blind optimism; it’s wandering with intention. It’s saying: I don’t know exactly how we get from here to better, but I’m willing to look, to try, to pay attention, to take one small step and then another. Cynicism is easy; it asks nothing of you. Hope asks everything, and gives everything back.

So here is my wandering wish for you, whoever you are reading this over cold tea or on a train or late at night when you should be sleeping:

May you have enough slowness to notice dust in sunlight. May you take the long way home sometimes. May you learn the name of one bird and one tree near you. May you let yourself be bored and see what grows there. May you look up at the moon and feel, for a second, both tiny and immense — because you are both, and that’s not a contradiction, that’s the truth.

May you be noticed, truly noticed, by someone who loves you, and may you offer that same rare generosity to others. May you remember that your ordinary days are someone’s future treasure — your kitchen sounds, your laugh, your walk. Live them with that tenderness in mind, not with pressure to be perfect, but with permission to be present.

And when time feels too fast, as it will, may you know how to slow it from the inside: with newness, with gratitude, with wide-open attention. Collect moments the way children collect shells — not for value, but for wonder. This one is ridged. This one is pink inside. This one sounds like the sea.

The world is loud and broken and beautiful, often all at once. It needs people who are willing to wander through it with eyes open, hearts soft, hands ready. Not heroes every minute, just humans, paying attention.

My tea is cold. The light has moved off the dust and onto the wall. The day is waiting, with its emails and errands and noise. I’ll drink the cold tea anyway — it’s still tea, still a small comfort — and I’ll step outside and see what the sky is doing. I suggest you do the same, in your own way, in your own place.

Look up. Notice. Wander. Begin again.

It will be built by millions of small attentions: people who noticed a problem on their block and cared enough to act, people who listened across difference instead of shouting, people who chose repair over discard — of objects, of relationships, of ecosystems.

Hope gets a bad rap as naive. But real hope isn’t blind optimism; it’s wandering with intention. It’s saying: I don’t know exactly how we get from here to better, but I’m willing to look, to try, to pay attention, to take one small step and then another. Cynicism is easy; it asks nothing of you. Hope asks everything, and gives everything back.

So here is my wandering wish for you, whoever you are reading this over cold tea or on a train or late at night when you should be sleeping:

May you have enough slowness to notice dust in sunlight. May you take the long way home sometimes. May you learn the name of one bird and one tree near you. May you let yourself be bored and see what grows there. May you look up at the moon and feel, for a second, both tiny and immense — because you are both, and that’s not a contradiction, that’s the truth.

May you be noticed, truly noticed, by someone who loves you, and may you offer that same rare generosity to others. May you remember that your ordinary days are someone’s future treasure — your kitchen sounds, your laugh, your walk. Live them with that tenderness in mind, not with pressure to be perfect, but with permission to be present.

And when time feels too fast, as it will, may you know how to slow it from the inside: with newness, with gratitude, with wide-open attention. Collect moments the way children collect shells — not for value, but for wonder. This one is ridged. This one is pink inside. This one sounds like the sea.

The world is loud and broken and beautiful, often all at once. It needs people who are willing to wander through it with eyes open, hearts soft, hands ready. Not heroes every minute, just humans, paying attention.

My tea is cold. The light has moved off the dust and onto the wall. The day is waiting, with its emails and errands and noise. I’ll drink the cold tea anyway — it’s still tea, still a small comfort — and I’ll step outside and see what the sky is doing. I suggest you do the same, in your own way, in your own place.

Look up. Notice. Wander. Begin again.
